headline: Resilience Fails at the Service Point
deck: A refrigeration attack, cyclone damage and strikes near Hormuz show why an incident’s consequences turn on physical systems.
body: Dozens of supermarkets in seven European countries were hit by a cyberattack affecting refrigerators and freezers, the BBC reported. [E1]
Sabcobel, a Belgian manufacturer of some affected refrigerators, said their evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm. [E2]
Cyclone Murasu uprooted thousands of trees, damaged hundreds of electric poles, wrecked fishing boats and inundated parts of coastal Andhra Pradesh, the New Indian Express reported. [E3]
The India Meteorological Department said Murasu crossed near Ongole with gusts reaching 120 kmph. [E5]

The United States launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island late Monday, hours after Vice-President JD Vance said he was optimistic about diplomatic efforts to end the war, the Guardian reported. This paper’s previous Hormuz coverage concerned an announced maritime warning; the new established fact is the strike. [E4]

**The desk's reading.** The confirmed common ground is narrower than it first looked: public systems meet people through equipment and routes that can be damaged, altered or put under pressure. The refrigerator and the electric pole make that fact visible; the Qeshm report establishes a strike, not a failure of civilian or commercial service. The stronger competing reading is that these are two service disruptions and one military event gathered by a theme, with no shared civic vulnerability demonstrated.

**The next test.** By 15:00 UTC, company updates should show whether affected refrigeration is operating again, and Andhra authorities or utilities should show whether damaged power and transport links are being restored. Reporting from Qeshm should establish a concrete effect on a civilian or commercial service, or show none. Prompt restoration in the first two cases and no such consequence from the strike would leave only a loose grouping. Continued service interruptions, with a documented service effect from Qeshm, would support the narrower reading that resilience is decided at the physical point of service.
